notes:
1. Meaning of a State

  • A State is a constitutionally recognised territorial and governmental unit within the Indian Union.

A State ordinarily possesses:

  • Defined territory.
  • Governor.
  • Elected government.
  • Legislature.
  • Administrative institutions.
  • Legislative authority over constitutionally assigned subjects.
  • Representation in Parliament.
  • A State forms an important constituent unit of Indian federalism.
📌 Must-Memorise

State → Constitutional Territorial + Governmental Unit

2. State Is Not a Sovereign Country

  • An Indian State is not an internationally sovereign political entity.
  • It cannot independently conduct foreign relations as a sovereign country.
  • It cannot independently declare war.
  • It cannot enter international treaties as a sovereign State.
  • It cannot issue a separate national citizenship.
  • It cannot constitutionally secede from India.
  • Sovereignty belongs to India as a whole.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Indian State ≠ Sovereign Country

3. Constitutional Authority of States

  • State governments do not ordinarily function merely as administrative agents of the Union.
  • They derive constitutional authority directly from the Constitution in matters assigned to them.

Their constitutional status is therefore different from:

  • District administrations.
  • Municipalities.
  • Panchayats.
  • Ordinary administrative departments.
  • During normal constitutional conditions, States exercise authority in constitutionally assigned fields.
📌 Must-Memorise

State Government → Constitutional Authority
District/Municipality/Panchayat → Not Equivalent to State

4. States as Constituent Units of the Union

  • Article 1 declares India to be a Union of States.
  • States together form part of one constitutional political order.
  • Indian federalism was not created by a treaty among previously sovereign States.
  • States therefore do not possess a constitutional right to leave the Union.
  • State boundaries and territories may be reorganised by Parliament under Article 3.
  • This creates the distinctive Indian arrangement of a permanent Union with reorganisable States.
📌 Must-Memorise

Union → Permanent
States → Reorganisable

5. State Autonomy

  • State autonomy means that a State may exercise authority in constitutionally assigned areas.
  • It does not mean complete sovereignty.
  • It does not mean independence from the Constitution.
  • A State cannot reject a constitutionally valid Union law merely because it disagrees with it.
  • A State cannot claim a constitutional right to secession.
  • State autonomy operates within the constitutional distribution of powers.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

State Autonomy ≠ State Sovereignty

6. State Identity within One Union

States may possess distinct:

  • Languages.
  • Cultural traditions.
  • Historical identities.
  • Regional priorities.
  • Administrative needs.
  • The Constitution accommodates these differences while maintaining one Union.
  • Federalism therefore combines regional diversity with national unity.

7. India as a Holding-Together Federation

  • India is often described as a holding-together federation.
  • The Centre possesses significant constitutional strength.
  • State boundaries can be altered by Parliament.
  • The constitutional system was not formed through a compact among sovereign States.
  • This differs from classical coming-together federations.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

India → Holding-Together Federation

8. Part VI — The States

  • Part VI of the Constitution is titled “The States.”
  • It extends from Article 152 to Article 237.
  • It provides the principal constitutional framework for State institutions.
  • Part VI begins with Article 152.
  • Article 153 provides for the office of Governor.
📌 Must-Memorise

Part VI → The States
Articles → 152–237

9. What Part VI Covers

Part VI broadly deals with:

  • Governor.
  • State Executive.
  • Council of Ministers.
  • Advocate-General.
  • State Legislature.
  • Legislative procedure.
  • Governor's legislative powers.
  • High Courts.
  • Subordinate Courts.

10. Common Constitutional Model of States

Most States broadly follow the same constitutional structure:

  • Governor as constitutional head.
  • Chief Minister as real political executive.
  • Council of Ministers.
  • State Legislature.
  • High Court.
  • Subordinate judiciary.
  • State administration.
  • The State parliamentary system broadly reflects the Union parliamentary model.

11. One Governor for Two or More States

  • Article 153 permits the same person to be appointed Governor for two or more States.
  • Appointment of one person as Governor of multiple States does not merge those States.
  • Each State retains its separate constitutional identity and government.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 153 → One Governor May Serve Two or More States

12. Common High Court

  • A common High Court may serve two or more States.
  • A common High Court may also serve a State and one or more Union Territories.
  • Sharing a High Court does not eliminate the separate constitutional identity of the States concerned.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Common Governor/High Court ≠ Merger of States

13. First Schedule and States

The First Schedule specifies:

  • Names of States.
  • Territorial descriptions of States.
  • Names of Union Territories.
  • Territorial descriptions of Union Territories.
  • Inclusion in the First Schedule formally identifies a territorial unit as a State or Union Territory under the Constitution.
  • Territorial reorganisation may require corresponding changes in the First Schedule.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Schedule → States + Union Territories + Territorial Descriptions

14. Present Number of States

The attached reference records that India presently has:

  • 28 States.
  • 8 Union Territories.
  • The chapter should distinguish States from Union Territories because their constitutional positions are not identical.
📌 Must-Memorise

India → 28 States + 8 Union Territories

16. Constitutional Significance of Statehood

  • Statehood gives a territorial unit full status as a constituent State within the federal framework.

A State ordinarily possesses:

  • Governor.
  • Elected State government.
  • State Legislature.
  • Legislative authority over constitutionally assigned subjects.
  • Representation in Rajya Sabha.
  • Statehood is constitutionally distinct from Union Territory status.

17. Formation and Reorganisation of States

Under Article 3, Parliament may:

  • Create a new State.
  • Divide an existing State.
  • Merge States or parts of States.
  • Increase the area of a State.
  • Diminish the area of a State.
  • Alter State boundaries.
  • Change the name of a State.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 3 → Formation + Area + Boundary + Name

18. State Consultation in Reorganisation

  • Where Article 3 requires it, the affected State Legislature must be given an opportunity to express its views.
  • The State Legislature may support, oppose or suggest changes to the proposal.
  • Its views are not binding on Parliament.
  • The Constitution requires consultation, not consent.
  • A State therefore has no constitutional veto over reorganisation.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

State Legislature → Views
Parliament → Final Authority

19. Common Grounds for State Reorganisation

Indian States have historically been reorganised on grounds such as:

  • Language.
  • Regional identity.
  • Administrative convenience.
  • Tribal identity.
  • Economic development.
  • Geographic accessibility.
  • Public demand.
  • Political settlement.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

State Formation → Not Based on Language Alone

20. Examples of Different Bases of State Formation

  • Andhra State → Linguistic demand.
  • Nagaland → Tribal and political settlement.
  • Haryana → Linguistic and administrative reorganisation.
  • Chhattisgarh → Regional and developmental considerations.
  • Jharkhand → Tribal and regional movement.
  • Telangana → Regional Statehood movement.

21. Renaming of States

Parliament has changed State names through law.

Important examples include:

  • Madras State → Tamil Nadu.
  • Mysore → Karnataka.
  • Uttaranchal → Uttarakhand.
  • Orissa → Odisha.
  • A State's constitutional existence does not guarantee permanent retention of its original name.
📌 Tamil Nadu Must-Memorise

Madras State → Tamil Nadu

22. Statehood and Territorial Permanence

  • Statehood is a constitutionally recognised level of government.

But a State's specific:

  • Name.
  • Area.
  • Boundary.
  • Territorial composition

may be altered through constitutional procedure.

  • Therefore, Statehood does not create permanent territorial immunity.

23. States Created from Union Territories

Several present States earlier existed under Union Territory or centrally administered arrangements.

Examples include:

  • Himachal Pradesh.
  • Manipur.
  • Tripura.
  • Mizoram.
  • Arunachal Pradesh.
  • Goa.
  • Union Territory status may therefore precede full Statehood.

24. Himachal Pradesh, Manipur and Tripura

  • Himachal Pradesh became a full State in 1971.
  • Manipur became a State in 1972.
  • Tripura became a State in 1972.
  • These territories had previously been administered under centrally controlled or Union Territory arrangements.
📌 Must-Memorise

Himachal Pradesh → 1971
Manipur + Tripura → 1972

25. Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa

  • Mizoram was a Union Territory before becoming a State in 1987.
  • Arunachal Pradesh was also a Union Territory before Statehood in 1987.
  • Goa had formed part of the Union Territory of Goa, Daman and Diu.
  • Goa became a State in 1987.
📌 Must-Memorise

1987 → Mizoram + Arunachal Pradesh + Goa

26. Sikkim's Distinct Constitutional Route

  • Sikkim followed a special constitutional process.
  • The Thirty-Fifth Constitutional Amendment gave Sikkim an associated-status arrangement.
  • The Thirty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment, 1975 made Sikkim a full State.
  • Article 371F contains special constitutional provisions relating to Sikkim.
📌 Must-Memorise

35th Amendment → Sikkim Associated Status
36th Amendment → Sikkim Statehood → 1975

27. Why Statehood May Be Granted

Statehood may provide:

  • Greater political autonomy.
  • Elected State government.
  • Full State legislative status.
  • Representation as a State in Rajya Sabha.
  • Greater regional self-government.
  • A stronger constitutional position than ordinary Union Territory administration.

28. Statehood vs Union Territory Legislature

  • Some Union Territories may possess a Legislative Assembly and Council of Ministers.
  • This does not make them constitutionally identical to States.
  • State status and Union Territory status remain legally distinct.
  • The existence of a Legislature alone is not sufficient to make a territory a State.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

UT with Legislature ≠ State

29. Constitutional Equality of States

  • All States are constituent units of the Indian Union.
  • No State is constitutionally sovereign over another State.
  • However, constitutional equality does not mean that all States are identical in population, size or representation.

30. Unequal Size of States

States differ considerably in:

  • Population.
  • Territory.
  • Economic capacity.
  • Number of districts.
  • Legislative strength.
  • Parliamentary representation.
  • Administrative needs.
  • Constitutional federalism accommodates this variation.

31. Lok Sabha Representation of States

  • States do not receive equal representation in the Lok Sabha.
  • Lok Sabha representation is broadly related to population and constitutional allocation.
  • Large and small States therefore have different numbers of Lok Sabha seats.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Lok Sabha → States Not Equally Represented

32. Rajya Sabha Representation of States

  • Rajya Sabha does not give every State an equal number of seats.
  • This differs from the United States Senate.
  • Representation is broadly related to population.
  • Allocation of seats is contained in the Fourth Schedule.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fourth Schedule → Rajya Sabha Seat Allocation

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Rajya Sabha → Equal State Representation? → No

33. Constitutional Equality vs Identical Treatment

Equal constitutional status does not require identical:

  • Parliamentary representation.
  • Financial allocation.
  • Legislative size.
  • Administrative arrangements.
  • Special constitutional provisions.
  • Different arrangements may be justified by history, geography or social conditions.

34. Symmetrical Federalism

  • Symmetrical federalism gives substantially similar constitutional powers and institutional arrangements to all constituent units.
  • A perfectly symmetrical federation would treat its constituent units in broadly identical constitutional terms.

35. Asymmetrical Federalism

  • Asymmetrical federalism allows special constitutional arrangements for particular States or regions.
  • India contains important asymmetrical features.

Special provisions may respond to:

  • Tribal customs.
  • Traditional law.
  • Land ownership.
  • Religious and social practices.
  • Regional underdevelopment.
  • Local employment.
  • Distinct political history.
  • Border conditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Indian Federalism → Contains Asymmetrical Features

36. Constitutional Sources of Asymmetry

Important examples include:

  • Articles 371 to 371J.
  • Fifth Schedule.
  • Sixth Schedule.
  • Special regional development boards.
  • Autonomous District Councils.
  • Different institutional arrangements for particular States.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Special Provision ≠ Separate Sovereignty

37. Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions

  • Constitutional terms such as temporary, transitional and special should not be treated as identical.
  • Most provisions under Articles 371 to 371J are special provisions linked to particular States.
  • Such provisions provide constitutional accommodation within the Union.
  • They do not confer independence on the State concerned.

38. Article 371 — Maharashtra and Gujarat

  • Article 371 contains special provisions relating to Maharashtra and Gujarat.
  • The President may assign special responsibility to the Governor regarding development boards.
  • The purpose is to address regional imbalance and equitable development.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 371 → Maharashtra + Gujarat

39. Development Boards under Article 371

For Maharashtra, development boards may relate to:

  • Vidarbha.
  • Marathwada.
  • Rest of Maharashtra.

For Gujarat:

  • Saurashtra.
  • Kutch.
  • Rest of Gujarat.
  • The objective is balanced intra-State development.
📌 Must-Memorise

371 → Regional Development Boards

40. Objectives of Article 371

Article 371 arrangements seek:

  • Equitable allocation of development funds.
  • Balanced regional development.
  • Technical and vocational education.
  • Fair opportunities in State government employment.
  • Reduction of intra-State regional imbalance.

41. Article 371A — Nagaland

  • Article 371A contains special constitutional protections for Nagaland.
  • Certain Acts of Parliament on specified subjects do not automatically apply to Nagaland unless the Nagaland Legislative Assembly passes a resolution.
  • The provision reflects negotiated constitutional accommodation and protection of Naga customary institutions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 371A → Nagaland

42. Protected Subjects under Article 371A

The protected matters include:

  • Religious or social practices of the Nagas.
  • Naga customary law and procedure.
  • Administration of civil and criminal justice involving Naga customary law.
  • Ownership and transfer of land and its resources.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

371A → Naga Customs + Customary Law + Land and Resources

43. Governor's Role under Article 371A

  • The Governor has a special constitutional responsibility concerning law and order under the conditions specified in Article 371A.
  • The Article historically also contains special provisions connected with the Tuensang area.
  • These provisions reflect Nagaland's distinct historical and political integration.

44. Article 371B — Assam

  • Article 371B contains a special provision for Assam.
  • The President may provide for a committee of the Assam Legislative Assembly.
  • The committee includes representatives from specified tribal areas.
  • Its purpose is to ensure legislative attention to tribal-area concerns.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 371B → Assam → Tribal-Area Committee

45. Article 371C — Manipur

  • Article 371C contains special provisions for the hill areas of Manipur.
  • The President may provide for a Hill Areas Committee of the Manipur Legislative Assembly.
  • The Committee consists of members elected from the hill areas.
  • The Governor has a special responsibility regarding proper functioning of this arrangement.
  • The Governor may report to the President regarding administration of the hill areas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 371C → Manipur → Hill Areas Committee

46. Assam vs Manipur Special Provisions

  • Article 371B → Assam.
  • Article 371C → Manipur.
  • Assam → Tribal-area committee in State Assembly.
  • Manipur → Hill Areas Committee + Governor's special reporting role.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

371B → Assam
371C → Manipur

47. Article 371D — Andhra Pradesh and Telangana

  • Article 371D seeks equitable opportunities and facilities for people from different regions.

It relates especially to:

  • Public employment.
  • Education.
  • Local cadres.
  • Regional access.
  • Administrative arrangements.
  • The provision now has relevance to the constitutional framework involving Andhra Pradesh and Telangana.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 371D → Andhra Pradesh/Telangana → Education + Public Employment

48. Presidential Orders under Article 371D

The President may make orders relating to:

  • Organisation of local cadres.
  • Local-area preferences.
  • Admission to educational institutions.
  • Public-employment arrangements.
  • The objective is equitable regional opportunity.

49. Administrative Tribunal under Article 371D

  • Article 371D historically provided for an Administrative Tribunal dealing with specified service matters.
  • A portion of the earlier arrangement was affected by the Supreme Court decision in P. Sambamurthy v. State of Andhra Pradesh.
  • The case is relevant to the constitutional limits placed on exclusion of judicial review.
🧭 TNPSC Key Link

P. Sambamurthy → Article 371D

50. Article 371E — Central University

  • Article 371E authorises Parliament to establish a Central University in Andhra Pradesh.
  • It is distinct from Article 371D.
📌 Must-Memorise

371D → Regional Employment/Education
371E → Central University in Andhra Pradesh

51. Article 371F — Sikkim

  • Article 371F contains special provisions for Sikkim.
  • Sikkim became a full State in 1975 through the Thirty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment.
  • The Article provides for constitutional continuity during Sikkim's integration into India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 371F → Sikkim

52. Features of Article 371F

Article 371F deals with matters including:

  • Composition of the Legislative Assembly.
  • Continuity of existing laws.
  • Representation.
  • Protection of different sections of the population.
  • Administrative transition.
  • Legislative arrangements.
  • Existing laws could continue until altered or repealed by the competent authority.

53. Governor's Responsibility in Sikkim

Article 371F gives the Governor a special responsibility relating to:

  • Peace.
  • Equitable social and economic advancement of different sections of the population.
  • The provision reflects Sikkim's distinct historical integration.

54. Article 371G — Mizoram

  • Article 371G contains special provisions for Mizoram.
  • Acts of Parliament relating to specified subjects do not automatically apply unless the Mizoram Legislative Assembly passes a resolution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 371G → Mizoram

55. Protected Subjects under Article 371G

Protected matters include:

  • Religious or social practices of the Mizos.
  • Mizo customary law and procedure.
  • Administration of justice involving Mizo customary law.
  • Ownership and transfer of land.
  • The structure closely resembles some protections available to Nagaland under Article 371A.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

371A → Nagaland
371G → Mizoram
Both → Customary Practices + Land Protection

56. Mizoram Legislative Assembly

  • Article 371G also contains a constitutional minimum-size provision relating to the Mizoram Legislative Assembly.
  • The special constitutional arrangement therefore includes both cultural protections and legislative-institutional provisions.

57. Article 371H — Arunachal Pradesh

  • Article 371H applies to Arunachal Pradesh.
  • The Governor has a special responsibility concerning law and order.
  • Within the constitutional scope of that responsibility, the Governor may exercise individual judgment.
  • The President may later direct that the special responsibility cease when it is no longer necessary.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 371H → Arunachal Pradesh → Law and Order

58. Arunachal Pradesh Assembly Strength

  • Article 371H provides that the Legislative Assembly of Arunachal Pradesh shall have not fewer than 30 members.
📌 Must-Memorise

Arunachal Pradesh Assembly → Minimum 30

59. Article 371I — Goa

  • Article 371I applies to Goa.
  • It provides that the Goa Legislative Assembly shall consist of not fewer than 30 members.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 371I → Goa → Minimum 30 Assembly Members

60. Article 371J — Karnataka

  • Article 371J contains special provisions for Karnataka.
  • It focuses on the historically disadvantaged Hyderabad-Karnataka region, now commonly referred to as Kalyana Karnataka.
  • The provision seeks to reduce regional imbalance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 371J → Karnataka → Kalyana Karnataka

61. Development Measures under Article 371J

Article 371J supports:

  • Separate development board.
  • Equitable allocation of development funds.
  • Educational opportunities.
  • Vocational training.
  • Employment opportunities.
  • Regional infrastructure.
  • Local reservation arrangements subject to constitutional and statutory rules.

62. Article 371 Series — Master Mapping

  • Article 371 → Maharashtra and Gujarat.
  • Article 371A → Nagaland.
  • Article 371B → Assam.
  • Article 371C → Manipur.
  • Article 371D → Andhra Pradesh and Telangana-related regional arrangements.
  • Article 371E → Central University in Andhra Pradesh.
  • Article 371F → Sikkim.
  • Article 371G → Mizoram.
  • Article 371H → Arunachal Pradesh.
  • Article 371I → Goa.
  • Article 371J → Karnataka.

63. Fifth Schedule — Scheduled Areas

  • The Fifth Schedule deals with administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes.
  • It broadly applies outside the specific tribal areas governed by the Sixth Schedule.
  • The President plays a role in declaring Scheduled Areas.
  • The Governor has special responsibilities.
  • A Tribes Advisory Council forms part of the framework.
  • Special regulation may protect tribal land and control money-lending.
  • Laws may be adapted to local conditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fifth Schedule → Scheduled Areas + Tribes Advisory Council

64. Sixth Schedule — Tribal Areas

The Sixth Schedule applies to specified tribal areas in:

  • Assam.
  • Meghalaya.
  • Tripura.
  • Mizoram.
  • It creates a stronger autonomous institutional framework than the Fifth Schedule.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sixth Schedule → Assam + Meghalaya + Tripura + Mizoram

65. Autonomous District and Regional Councils

The Sixth Schedule provides for:

  • Autonomous District Councils.
  • Regional Councils.
  • Legislative powers in specified subjects.
  • Administrative powers.
  • Recognition of customary law.
  • Local taxation.
  • Local administration.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Sixth Schedule → Greater Institutional Autonomy

66. Fifth Schedule vs Sixth Schedule

Fifth Schedule:

  • Scheduled Areas.
  • Governor's role.
  • Tribes Advisory Council.
  • Wider State administrative structure.

Sixth Schedule:

  • Autonomous District Councils.
  • Regional Councils.
  • Greater institutional autonomy.
  • Limited to specified northeastern tribal areas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 244 → Constitutional Link to Fifth and Sixth Schedules

67. Inter-State Boundary Changes

  • Parliament may alter State boundaries under Article 3.
  • A State Legislature cannot independently change its constitutional boundary with another State.
  • Parliamentary legislation is required.
  • States therefore do not possess unilateral authority over inter-State boundaries.

68. Causes of Inter-State Boundary Disputes

Boundary disputes may arise because of:

  • Linguistic claims.
  • Historical administrative boundaries.
  • Village-level territorial claims.
  • Access to rivers and resources.
  • Cultural identity.
  • Earlier reorganisation settlements.

69. Methods of Resolving Boundary Disputes

Boundary disputes may be addressed through:

  • Negotiation.
  • Union mediation.
  • Commissions.
  • Parliamentary legislation.
  • Political agreements.
  • Judicial proceedings where legally maintainable.
  • The Ministry of Home Affairs deals with important State-reorganisation and inter-State boundary matters at the Union level.

70. Boundary Dispute vs Inter-State Water Dispute

Boundary dispute:

  • Concerns territorial jurisdiction.

Inter-State water dispute:

  • Concerns use, control or distribution of river water.
  • These involve different constitutional and legal mechanisms.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Boundary Dispute ≠ Water Dispute

71. Zonal Councils

  • Zonal Councils are statutory bodies.
  • They are not constitutional bodies.
  • They were created under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
  • Their purpose is to promote regional cooperation among States.
📌 Must-Memorise

Zonal Councils → Statutory
Created by → States Reorganisation Act, 1956

72. Five Zonal Councils

The five Zonal Councils are:

  • Northern Zonal Council.
  • Central Zonal Council.
  • Eastern Zonal Council.
  • Western Zonal Council.
  • Southern Zonal Council.
📌 Must-Memorise

Five Zonal Councils → North + Central + East + West + South

73. North Eastern Council

  • The North Eastern Council is separate from the five Zonal Councils.
  • It was created under a different statute.
  • It should not be counted as the sixth Zonal Council.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

North Eastern Council ≠ Zonal Council

74. Chairperson and Membership of Zonal Councils

  • The Union Home Minister serves as Chairman of the Zonal Councils.

Membership broadly includes:

  • Chief Ministers of States in the zone.
  • Administrators or Lieutenant Governors of relevant Union Territories.
  • Other ministers as provided by law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Zonal Councils Chairman → Union Home Minister

75. Objectives of Zonal Councils

Zonal Councils promote:

  • Inter-State cooperation.
  • Resolution of regional disputes.
  • Border coordination.
  • Economic and social planning.
  • Transport cooperation.
  • Security coordination.
  • Exchange of administrative experience.
  • Their role is primarily advisory and consultative.

76. Zonal Council vs Inter-State Council

Zonal Council:

  • Statutory body.
  • Regional.
  • Created under States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

Inter-State Council:

  • Constitutional basis.
  • Article 263.
  • National-level Centre–State and inter-State consultation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Zonal Council → Statutory
Inter-State Council → Article 263

77. State Capitals

  • The Constitution does not prescribe one uniform method for selecting every State capital.

A State capital may be determined through:

  • Reorganisation law.
  • State legislation.
  • Executive arrangement.
  • Historical practice.
  • Constitutional Statehood and choice of capital are therefore separate matters.

78. Shared Capital — Chandigarh

  • A city may serve as capital for more than one governmental unit.
  • Chandigarh serves as the capital of Punjab and Haryana.
  • Chandigarh itself remains a Union Territory.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chandigarh → Capital of Punjab + Haryana → Union Territory

79. Official Language of a State

  • A State Legislature may adopt one or more languages used in the State as its official language or languages.
  • Hindi may also be adopted.
  • English may continue for official purposes where law permits.
  • State official-language arrangements reflect India's linguistic diversity.

80. Language and Statehood

  • Linguistic considerations played a major role in State reorganisation after independence.
  • However, language is not the only basis for Statehood.
  • Every linguistic community does not possess a separate State.
  • A single State may contain several languages.
  • Regional identity, tribal considerations and administrative factors have also influenced State formation.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Language → Major Basis
Not Sole Basis of State Formation

81. State Symbols

States commonly adopt:

  • State animal.
  • State bird.
  • State flower.
  • State tree.
  • State emblem.
  • These are generally matters of State policy.
  • The Constitution does not impose one uniform set of State symbols on every State.
  • State symbols do not replace the legal and constitutional status of national symbols.

82. States vs Union Territories — Constitutional Position

States:

  • Constituent units of the federal system.
  • Possess constitutionally distributed legislative authority.
  • Ordinarily possess elected State governments.
  • Represented in Rajya Sabha.
  • Operate primarily under Part VI.

Union Territories:

  • Principally administered by the President.
  • Operate primarily under Part VIII and special provisions.
  • Parliament generally retains broader legislative and administrative authority.

83. Executive Difference — State vs Union Territory

State:

  • Governor serves as constitutional head.
  • Council of Ministers headed by Chief Minister exercises real political executive authority.

Union Territory:

  • Administrator or Lieutenant Governor represents the President.
  • Some UTs possess Councils of Ministers, but their constitutional position remains different from that of States.

84. Legislative Difference — State vs Union Territory

State:

  • State Legislature derives legislative competence from the constitutional distribution of legislative subjects.

Union Territory:

  • Parliament generally possesses broader legislative authority.
  • Some Union Territories possess Legislatures under special constitutional or statutory arrangements.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

UT Legislature ≠ State Legislature in Constitutional Status

85. Rajya Sabha Representation — States vs UTs

  • States receive representation in Rajya Sabha through the constitutional allocation in the Fourth Schedule.
  • Not every Union Territory is represented in the Rajya Sabha.
  • State representation is therefore a standard federal feature, whereas UT representation depends on constitutional and statutory arrangements.

86. Alteration of State and Union Territory Status

  • Parliament may convert a Union Territory into a State.
  • Parliament may reorganise a State into Union Territories.
  • Parliament may merge territorial units.
  • Parliament may divide territorial units.
  • Appropriate constitutional and statutory procedures must be followed.
  • Territorial status within the Indian Union is therefore constitutionally alterable.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

What is a State in the Indian Constitution? → A constitutionally recognised territorial and governmental unit of the Indian Union.

Is an Indian State internationally sovereign? → No.

Can a State conduct independent foreign relations? → No.

Can a State enter sovereign international treaties independently? → No.

Can a State issue separate national citizenship? → No.

Can a State secede from India? → No.

Where does sovereignty lie? → India as a whole.

Do State governments derive authority merely from the Union government? → No. They derive authority directly from the Constitution in assigned fields.

What does State autonomy mean? → Constitutional authority in assigned areas, not sovereignty.

Which Part deals principally with States? → Part VI.

Which Articles are covered by Part VI? → Articles 152–237.

Which Article deals with Governors of States? → Article 153.

Can one person be Governor of two or more States? → Yes.

Does a common Governor merge those States? → No.

Can two States share a High Court? → Yes.

Does a common High Court merge their constitutional identity? → No.

Which Schedule lists the States? → First Schedule.

How many States are recorded in the reference at present? → 28.

Which Article permits State reorganisation? → Article 3.

Does an affected State possess a veto over Article 3 reorganisation? → No.

What are important historical bases of State formation? → Language, regional identity, tribal identity, administrative convenience, economic development and political settlement.

Madras State was renamed as what? → Tamil Nadu.

Mysore was renamed as what? → Karnataka.

Uttaranchal was renamed as what? → Uttarakhand.

Orissa was renamed as what? → Odisha.

Can a Union Territory later become a State? → Yes.

When did Himachal Pradesh become a State? → 1971.

When did Manipur and Tripura become States? → 1972.

Which three obtained Statehood in 1987? → Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa.

Which Amendment made Sikkim a full State? → 36th Amendment, 1975.

Does a UT become a State merely because it has a Legislature? → No.

Do all States have equal Lok Sabha seats? → No.

Do all States have equal Rajya Sabha seats? → No.

Which Schedule allocates Rajya Sabha seats? → Fourth Schedule.

What is asymmetrical federalism? → Different constitutional arrangements for particular States or regions.

Which provisions are especially associated with special State arrangements? → Articles 371–371J.

Which States are covered by Article 371? → Maharashtra and Gujarat.

What is the main purpose of Article 371? → Regional development and equitable allocation within Maharashtra and Gujarat.

Which regions in Maharashtra are associated with development boards? → Vidarbha, Marathwada and the rest of Maharashtra.

Which Gujarat regions are associated with Article 371 development boards? → Saurashtra, Kutch and the rest of Gujarat.

Which Article applies to Nagaland? → Article 371A.

What does Article 371A protect? → Naga religious/social practices, customary law, customary justice, and land and resources.

Do parliamentary laws on protected Article 371A subjects automatically apply to Nagaland? → Not necessarily; a Nagaland Legislative Assembly resolution is constitutionally relevant.

Which Article applies to Assam? → Article 371B.

What does Article 371B provide? → A committee of the Assam Legislative Assembly involving specified tribal-area representatives.

Which Article applies to Manipur? → Article 371C.

What does Article 371C provide? → Hill Areas Committee and special Governor responsibilities.

Which Article concerns regional opportunities in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana? → Article 371D.

What areas does Article 371D concern? → Public employment, education, local cadres and regional opportunities.

Which case is associated with Article 371D? → P. Sambamurthy v. State of Andhra Pradesh.

What does Article 371E provide? → Parliament may establish a Central University in Andhra Pradesh.

Which Article applies to Sikkim? → Article 371F.

What does Article 371F broadly protect? → Legislative arrangements, continuity of laws, representation and administrative transition.

Which Article applies to Mizoram? → Article 371G.

What does Article 371G protect? → Mizo customs, customary law, administration of justice and land.

Which Article applies to Arunachal Pradesh? → Article 371H.

What special responsibility does the Arunachal Pradesh Governor have? → Law and order.

What is the constitutional minimum Assembly strength under Article 371H? → Not fewer than 30.

Which Article applies to Goa? → Article 371I.

What does Article 371I provide? → Goa Legislative Assembly shall have not fewer than 30 members.

Which Article applies to Karnataka? → Article 371J.

Which region is associated with Article 371J? → Kalyana Karnataka, formerly Hyderabad-Karnataka.

What is the purpose of Article 371J? → Regional development and improved access to education and employment.

Which Schedule deals with Scheduled Areas? → Fifth Schedule.

What important institution is associated with the Fifth Schedule? → Tribes Advisory Council.

Which Schedule provides Autonomous District Councils? → Sixth Schedule.

Which States are covered by the Sixth Schedule framework? → Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

Which Article is constitutionally connected with Fifth and Sixth Schedule areas? → Article 244.

Can a State Legislature independently change an inter-State boundary? → No.

Who has constitutional power to alter State boundaries? → Parliament.

Are Zonal Councils constitutional bodies? → No.

What are they? → Statutory bodies.

Which Act created the five Zonal Councils? → States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

How many Zonal Councils are there? → Five.

Name them. → Northern, Central, Eastern, Western and Southern.

Is the North Eastern Council one of the five Zonal Councils? → No.

Who chairs the Zonal Councils? → Union Home Minister.

Are Zonal Council decisions generally binding? → No; they are primarily advisory and consultative.

Which Article provides the constitutional basis for the Inter-State Council? → Article 263.

What is the difference between a Zonal Council and Inter-State Council? → Zonal Councils are statutory regional bodies; Inter-State Council has a constitutional basis under Article 263.

Can a State choose its capital only through a constitutional amendment? → No. Capital arrangements may arise through law, reorganisation legislation, executive arrangements or historical practice.

Which city is capital of both Punjab and Haryana? → Chandigarh.

What is Chandigarh's constitutional status? → Union Territory.

Can a State have more than one official language? → Yes.

Were all Indian States created purely on linguistic lines? → No.

Does every linguistic community have a separate State? → No.

Do State symbols have the same constitutional status as national symbols? → No.

What is the basic constitutional difference between States and Union Territories? → States are constituent units in the federal distribution of powers, whereas Union Territories are principally administered by the President under a different constitutional framework.

Does every Union Territory have Rajya Sabha representation? → No.

Can Parliament convert a Union Territory into a State? → Yes.

Can a State be reorganised into Union Territories? → Yes.
